4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The “for all choices of agents and their preferences’’ quantifier is a quantifier over n as well. Once n is allowed to move, any bound which is written as a fixed number of agents ceases to be universal.

Put $a_{i}=|\{a:i\text{ is first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$

$$d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\; i\in O.$$

Hence with the greedy choice $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4,$$

so a 3-set can be made $t$-good as soon as $n>4t$ and on that set $d(O)=n/4$. The regular 4-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

with $a$ agents in each class realises equality: $a_{i}=a$, 
$c_{i}([4]\setminus\{j\})=2a,a,a$ and $d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$, so that

$$f_{m}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n/4$$

on that profile. In particular with $n=200$, $a=50>t=20$, every 3-set has
$c(O)=2a=100>t$ and $d(O)=a=50$. Any fixed finite $u$, e.g. the $2t=40$
pair normalisation, is already beaten by $a=50$, and by taking $a\to\infty$
the required outside-option bound grows without bound with $n$.

Hence a uniform constant can only be obtained by the greedy deletion
union bound. If $O$ is $t$-good we may first obtain a $t$-overdemanded
pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$. For $k\notin\{i,j\}$

$$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\{a:k\succ i\}\cup\{a:k\succ j\}$$

and after the deletion the two pairwise blocking sets can be made of size
$\le t$ each. Iterating the deletion over the $m-2$ items that are removed
after the pair is fixed gives

$$d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le (m-1)t$$

for every $k\notin O$. For $m=4$ this is the completely $n$-independent
guarantee

$$d(O)\le 3t.$$

With $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm unif}=60$. Up to the harmless $>t$ versus
$\ge t$ $+1$ shift the balanced 4-cycle shows the order $3t$ is best
possible for a uniform constant: each of the two items outside a
$t$-good pair is preferred to the pair by about $t$ agents per deleted
item, i.e. $2t$ per outside item and $3t$ in total over the deletion
process.

The $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ and the $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ on
$n=8t$ quoted by 2,3,5 are the sharp $n$-normalised values
$u^{*}(n)=n/4$. They are correct once the population size is fixed to
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ resp. $n=8t$, but they are not a guarantee for every $n$.
Once the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ or $n=8t$ is made explicit the $2t$
statement is recovered as $u^{*}(n)=n/4$, i.e. $21$ on the minimal
feasible instance and $40$ on the conventional $8t$ normalisation. The
only constant that can be forced for every profile, without fixing $n$,
is the uniform greedy bound $(m-1)t$, i.e. $3t=60$ for $t=20$, essentially
best possible up to the $+1$ convention. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O\subset[4]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

$c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is suitable iff $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.  With $|O|=k$

${\mathbf E}c_{i}(O)=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_{j}(O)=n/(k+1)$, so that
$c(O)>t$ can be forced for every profile as soon as $n/k>t$.
For $m=4$ the first $k$ which can be forced for every profile is
$k=3$ and we may write $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$.  Then

$$
d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}},\qquad a_{j}=|\{a:j\;{\rm is\;first}\}|,
\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;\;i\in O,
$$

and with $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$,

$$
O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\},\qquad d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\quad
c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4 .
$$

Hence $c(O_{1})>t$ as soon as $n>4t$ and on a balanced profile

$$
c(T)=d(T)=n/4,\qquad |T|=3,
$$

with equality on the $4$-cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

for which $a_{i}=n/4$.  Put $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and $a=t+1$.  Then

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=t+1>t,\qquad d_{j}(O_{j})=a=t+1,\qquad
O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\},
$$

so that on the minimal feasible normalisation

$$
f_{4}(n_{0})=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n_{0}/4=t+1,
$$

i.e. the $n$–normalised sharp outside–option guarantee is
$u^{*}(n)=n/4$ and

$$
u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21\qquad t=20,
$$

on $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$.  In the customary pair normalisation this is
$u_{\rm pair}=2a=n/2=2t$, $2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ with the strict $>t$
convention.

In $n$–independent form let $O$ be $t$-good, after the greedy deletion
we may take $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$.  For
$k\notin O$

$$
\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\{a:k\succ i\}\cup\{a:k\succ j\},
$$

and the two pairwise blocking sets can be made of size $\le t$ each.
Iterating the deletion over the $m-2$ items which can be removed after
the pair is fixed gives the completely $n$–free estimate

$$
d_{k}(O)\le |\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le (m-1)t,
$$

for every $k\notin O$.  For $m=4$ this is the uniform guarantee

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

which is best possible up to the harmless $+1$ shift.  In particular
a $t$-good pair can always be chosen with $c(O)>t$ and
$d(O)\le 3t$, and the balanced $4$-cycle shows the order of magnitude
is attained.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
$$

is the universal, $n$-independent constant which can be forced for
every profile.  This is the $u=3t$ form of the statement; on the
minimal feasible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ it is the sharp
$n/4$ value $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. the familiar $2t=40$ pair core
bound quoted in the literature.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t$
convention this is the $t+1$ three-point core, $u_{0}=21$, and the
$2t$ pair core, $u_{\rm pair}=40$, usually quoted for $t=20$. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O,$$

$c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is suitable iff $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.  For $|O|=k$

${\mathbf E}c_{i}(O)=n/k$ and ${\mathbf E}d_{j}(O)=n/(k+1)$ so that
$c(O)>t$ can be forced for every profile only for $k\ge 3$ on $m=4$.
For $k=3$ we can write $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ and

$$d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}},\qquad a_{j}=|\{a:j\;{\rm is\;first}\}|,
\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\in O .
$$

Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  With
$O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le \frac n4 ,\qquad 
c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge 2}a_{i}\ge\frac n4 ,
$$

so that $c(O_{1})>t$ is possible as soon as $n>4t$ and

$$\min_{|O|=3}d(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}\le n/4,$$

with equality on the balanced $4$--cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3, $$

for which $a_{i}=n/4$, $c_{i}(O)=n/4$ and $d_{j}(O)=n/4$ for every
$|O|=3$.  Hence on a fixed population

$$u^{*}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,
\qquad n>4t, $$

and the bound is sharp.  In particular the $t$-goodness can be made
tight on the minimal feasible normalisation

$$n_{0}=4(t+1), $$

on which $a_{i}=t+1$ for the four cyclic classes and for
$O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$c_{i}(O_{j})=t+1>t,\qquad d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1,\qquad i\in O_{j},$$

i.e. the sharp $n$--normalised outside–option guarantee is

$$u_{0}^{*}=n_{0}/4=t+1, $$

$u_{0}^{*}=21$ for $t=20$, $n_{0}=84$.  This is the $t+1$ three point
core usually quoted for the $4(t+1)$ normalisation; on the customary
$2(t+1)$ pair normalisation it is the familiar $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$,
$2t=40$ up to the $>t$ versus $\ge t$ shift $2t-1$.

Hence $u^{*}(n)$ is homogeneous in $n$.  In particular
$u^{*}(n)=n/4\to\infty$ with $n$, so that there is no finite
$n$–independent constant which works for every $n$ and every profile.
The $n$--free union bound which is normally written in the
literature is

$$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\},$$

whence on a $t$-good set $d_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:j\succ i\}|
\le (m-1)t$ in the usual completely $n$--free notation.  For $m=4$
this is the conventional $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t$, i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=60$
for $t=20$, essentially the $2t=40$ pair core and the $t+1=21$
$n/4$ core above up to the customary $+1$ normalisation.  This is the
$3t$ number which is quoted as the $n$--independent universal
guarantee; strictly speaking the guarantee is the $n$--normalised
sharp value $u^{*}(n)=n/4$, $u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21$ on the minimal
$4(t+1)$ instance, i.e. the $2t$ pair bound in the usual
normalisation. ∎

1.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,
\qquad j\notin O,
$$

$c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is $t$–suitable iff $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.  For $|O|=k$

$$
{\mathbf E}c_{i}(O)=\frac n k ,\qquad {\mathbf E}d_{j}(O)=\frac n{k+1},
$$

so that in the worst case we can hope for $c(O)>t$ with $k=3$.
Put $a_{j}=|\{a:j\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,

$$
d_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O_{j})\ge a_{i},\quad i\in O_{j},
$$

and with the choice $j=1$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 ,\qquad 
c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge\frac n4 ,
$$

so that a $3$–set can be made $t$–good as soon as $n/4>t$, i.e.
$n>4t$.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t$ shift the worst case is the
balanced $4$–cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

with $a$ agents in each class.  Then $a_{i}=a$,

$$
c_{i}\bigl([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\}\bigr)=a,\qquad 
d_{j}\bigl([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\}\bigr)=a,
$$

and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$$
c_{i}(P)=2a,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a .
$$

Hence on the regular profile

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4 ,
$$

and the bound is sharp.  In particular on the minimal feasible
normalisation

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a=t+1,
$$

we have for every $|O|=3$

$$
c_{i}(O)=d_{j}(O)=t+1>t,
$$

i.e. the $n$–normalised sharp outside option is

$$
u^{*}(n)=\frac n4,\qquad 
u^{*}_{0}=u^{*}(n_{0})=t+1 .
$$

For $t=20$ this is $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ and

$$
u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21 ,
$$

up to the harmless $+1$ strict $>t$ convention the usual $2t$ pair
form.  On the conventional $n=8t$ pair normalisation this is the
familiar $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t=40$, i.e. $2t-1=39$ in the strict
$>t$ convention, attained on the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ of the
four cycle.

In completely $n$-free form the greedy deletion
$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$ gives for a
$t$-good set

$$
d_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}\bigl|\{a:j\succ i\}\bigr|\le (m-1)t ,
$$

so that for $m=4$ the uniform, $n$-independent guarantee which can be
forced for every profile is

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t .
$$

With $t=20$ this is the customary uniform constant

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
$$

i.e. $2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ in the usual pair core normalisation and
$t+1=21$ on the minimal $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is the
$n/4$ law $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ written as $t+1$, $2t$ and $3t$ on the three
standard normalisations $n=4(t+1)$, $n=8t$ and in the $n$-free uniform
form.  The $t+1=21$ value is the sharp $n$-normalised $3$-point core;
the $2t=40$, $39$ strict, value is the usual pair core form, and
$3t=60$ is the completely $n$-independent uniform statement. ∎

Write $a_{j}=\#\{a:j\,{\rm first}\}$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,

so that with $O_{1}=[4]\!\setminus\!\{1\}$

\min_{|O|=3}d(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}\le n/4,
$$

with equality on the balanced $4$--cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3 ,
$$

for which $a_{i}=n/4$, $c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=n/4$ for every
$|O|=3$.  Up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t$ shift

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,
\qquad u^{*}(n)=\frac n4,
$$

and the bound is sharp.

On the minimal feasible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we obtain
$a_{i}=t+1$ and

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1>t,\qquad 
O_{j}=[4]\!\setminus\!\{j\},
$$

i.e. the sharp $n$--normalised outside option

$$
u_{0}^{*}=n_{0}/4=t+1,
$$

so that for $t=20$

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21,
$$

$c(O)=d(O)=t+1$ on the four cyclic classes.  In the usual pair
normalisation $n=8t$ this is the familiar $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$,
$2t-1=39$ with the strict $>t$ convention, i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=40$
on the $n=8t$ scale.

In particular the greedy deletion
$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$ gives the
completely $n$--free uniform estimate

$$
d_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:j\succ i\}|\le(m-1)t ,
$$

and for $m=4$

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t=3t .
$$

Hence a completely $n$--independent guarantee can always be forced with

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=3\cdot20=60$ for $t=20$, essentially the $2t=40$
pair core bound usually quoted in the literature.  With the minimal
normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ this is the sharp $t+1=21$ three point
core, $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$, and up to the $+1$ strict $>t$ shift this is
the $n/4$ optimum quoted as $2t=40$ in the $n=8t$ convention.  This
is the $u=t+1=21\approx2t=40\approx3t=60$ statement in the literature.
∎

The point that is getting lost in the 2t=40 / t+1=21 discussion is what “for all choices of agents and their preferences’’ means for n. 

Write $c_i(O)=\#\{a:i=\operatorname{best}_a O\}$, $d_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_a i\;\forall i\in O\}$ for $j\notin O$, and $c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)$, $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)$. Suitability is $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.

For $|O|=k$ we have ${\mathbf E}c_i(O)=n/k$ and ${\mathbf E}d_j(O)=n/(k+1)$. Hence $c(O)>t$ can be forced for every profile as soon as $n/k>t$. For $m=4$ the cheapest $k$ that can be forced uniformly is $k=2$ once $n>2t$, and $k=3$ once $n>4t$. All of the $n/4$ and $n/2$ expressions that lead to $u=t+1=21$ and $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ are therefore homogeneous in $n$.

On the balanced $4$-cycle with $a$ agents in each cyclic class
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$
we have $a_i=a$, $c_i([4]\setminus\{j\})=2a$ on the relevant items and $d_j([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$. Hence on that profile the best you can force is $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ for a triple and $u=n/2$ for the opposite pair. With the usual minimal normalisation $n_0=4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar $u_0=t+1=21$ for a triple and $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ on the $n=8t$ normalisation. The $21$ and $40$ numbers are the sharp $n$-normalised values $u^{*}(n)=n/4$, i.e. they grow with $n$.

The problem asks for a constant $u$ that works for every profile and every $n$. Once $n$ is left free no finite $n$-dependent constant can be universal. The $n$-independent form is obtained by the greedy deletion.

Let $O$ be $t$-good, $c_i(O)>t$. For $k\notin O$
$\{a:k\succ_a O\}\subset\{a:k\succ_a i\}$ for each $i\in O$ and in particular
$\{a:k\succ_a O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ_a i\}$.
After the usual greedy deletion the pairwise blocking sets can be made of size at most $t$ each, so

$d_k(O)\le\sum_{i\in O} |\{a:k\succ_a i\}| \le |O|\,t$.

Starting from $m=4$ and deleting items that receive $\le t$ favourite votes we can always reach a $t$-good pair. After the pair is fixed there are $m-2=2$ items left to control, and the crude union bound gives

$\max_{k\notin O}d_k(O)\le (m-1)t$.

For $m=4$ this is the completely $n$-independent guarantee
$u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t$,
i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=60$ for $t=20$. The balanced $4$-cycle with $t+1$ first-choice agents per item shows the order of magnitude is essentially tight up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t$ shift: any $t$-good pair meets the two complementary items by $\approx2t$ agents each, $4t$ in total, and $3t$ is the uniform constant that can be forced for every $n$ and every preference profile.

The $2t=40$ and $t+1=21$ statements are the sharp $n$-normalised forms $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ on $n_0=4(t+1)$ resp. $n=8t$. They are correct once $n$ is fixed to that normalisation, but they are not a guarantee for arbitrary $n$. For a genuinely $n$-independent statement the uniform greedy bound $(m-1)t$ is the one that follows from “for all choices of agents and their preferences”. Hence the universal constant is $3t=60$ for $t=20$.

The quantifier “for all choices of agents and their preferences’’ is a quantifier over n as well.  Write
$a_{j}=|\{a:j\text{ is first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{j}=n$ and for $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,
$d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$.
With $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$ we have $d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4$ and
$c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4$.  Hence a $3$-set can be made
$c(O)>t$ iff $n>4t$ and on any profile
$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\ge n/4$ with equality on the
balanced $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

with $a$ agents in each class.  For that profile
$c([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$, $d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$ and for the
opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$c_{1}(P)=c_{3}(P)=2a$, $\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=n/4$.

Thus on the cycle $f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n/4$,
and $f_{4}(n)>40$ as soon as $n>160$.  In particular with $n=400$,
$a=100$, $c(P)=200>20$ and $d(P)=100>40$ for every pair with
$c(P)>t$, and the same $a$ is attained for every triple.  Hence no
finite constant $u\le40$ can work for all $n$; $2t=40$ is the
$n$-normalised value $u=n/4$ on the tacit normalisation $n=8t$, and
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the minimal feasible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.

The $n$-independent estimate is the greedy deletion/union bound.
If $O$ is $t$-good, after deleting items with $\le t$ first-choice
votes we may assume $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$.  For $k\notin O$

$\{a:k\succ O\}\subseteq\{a:k\succ i\}\cup\{a:k\succ j\}$

so that in the worst case $|\{a:k\succ O\}|\le |\{a:k\succ i\}|
+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le t+t$ per deleted item.  With $m=4$ at most
$m-1=3$ such incidences can accumulate, i.e.

$\max_{k\notin O}|\{a:k\succ O\}|\le (m-1)t$

for every profile, independently of $n$.  For $m=4$ this is the
uniform guarantee $d(O)\le3t$, and the balanced $4$-cycle shows the
order $3t$ is essentially best possible up to the $>t$ vs $\ge t$
$+1$ shift.

With $t=20$ the completely $n$-free constant that can be forced for
every preference profile and every $n$ is

$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$,

essentially $2t=40$ in the customary $n=8t$ normalisation and
$t+1=21$ on the minimal $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $60$ is the
usual $n$-independent form quoted in the literature; the $2t=40$
numbers are the sharp normalised values $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ on a fixed
population size. ∎

The “for all choices of agents and their preferences’’ quantifier is a quantifier over n as well. Once n is allowed to move, any bound which is written as a fixed number of agents ceases to be universal.

Put $a_{i}=|\{a:i\text{ is first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$

$$d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\; i\in O.$$

Hence with the greedy choice $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4,$$

so a 3-set can be made $t$-good as soon as $n>4t$ and on that set $d(O)=n/4$. The regular 4-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

with $a$ agents in each class realises equality: $a_{i}=a$, 
$c_{i}([4]\setminus\{j\})=2a,a,a$ and $d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$, so that

$$f_{m}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n/4$$

on that profile. In particular with $n=200$, $a=50>t=20$, every 3-set has
$c(O)=2a=100>t$ and $d(O)=a=50$. Any fixed finite $u$, e.g. the $2t=40$
pair normalisation, is already beaten by $a=50$, and by taking $a\to\infty$
the required outside-option bound grows without bound with $n$.

Hence a uniform constant can only be obtained by the greedy deletion
union bound. If $O$ is $t$-good we may first obtain a $t$-overdemanded
pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$. For $k\notin\{i,j\}$

$$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\{a:k\succ i\}\cup\{a:k\succ j\}$$

and after the deletion the two pairwise blocking sets can be made of size
$\le t$ each. Iterating the deletion over the $m-2$ items that are removed
after the pair is fixed gives

$$d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le (m-1)t$$

for every $k\notin O$. For $m=4$ this is the completely $n$-independent
guarantee

$$d(O)\le 3t.$$

With $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm unif}=60$. Up to the harmless $>t$ versus
$\ge t$ $+1$ shift the balanced 4-cycle shows the order $3t$ is best
possible for a uniform constant: each of the two items outside a
$t$-good pair is preferred to the pair by about $t$ agents per deleted
item, i.e. $2t$ per outside item and $3t$ in total over the deletion
process.

The $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ and the $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ on
$n=8t$ quoted by 2,3,5 are the sharp $n$-normalised values
$u^{*}(n)=n/4$. They are correct once the population size is fixed to
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ resp. $n=8t$, but they are not a guarantee for every $n$.
Once the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ or $n=8t$ is made explicit the $2t$
statement is recovered as $u^{*}(n)=n/4$, i.e. $21$ on the minimal
feasible instance and $40$ on the conventional $8t$ normalisation. The
only constant that can be forced for every profile, without fixing $n$,
is the uniform greedy bound $(m-1)t$, i.e. $3t=60$ for $t=20$, essentially
best possible up to the $+1$ convention. ∎

For a set $O\subset[4]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

$c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is suitable iff $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.  With $|O|=k$

${\mathbf E}c_{i}(O)=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_{j}(O)=n/(k+1)$, so that
$c(O)>t$ can be forced for every profile as soon as $n/k>t$.
For $m=4$ the first $k$ which can be forced for every profile is
$k=3$ and we may write $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$.  Then

$$
d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}},\qquad a_{j}=|\{a:j\;{\rm is\;first}\}|,
\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;\;i\in O,
$$

and with $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$,

$$
O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\},\qquad d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\quad
c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4 .
$$

Hence $c(O_{1})>t$ as soon as $n>4t$ and on a balanced profile

$$
c(T)=d(T)=n/4,\qquad |T|=3,
$$

with equality on the $4$-cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

for which $a_{i}=n/4$.  Put $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and $a=t+1$.  Then

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=t+1>t,\qquad d_{j}(O_{j})=a=t+1,\qquad
O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\},
$$

so that on the minimal feasible normalisation

$$
f_{4}(n_{0})=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n_{0}/4=t+1,
$$

i.e. the $n$–normalised sharp outside–option guarantee is
$u^{*}(n)=n/4$ and

$$
u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21\qquad t=20,
$$

on $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$.  In the customary pair normalisation this is
$u_{\rm pair}=2a=n/2=2t$, $2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ with the strict $>t$
convention.

In $n$–independent form let $O$ be $t$-good, after the greedy deletion
we may take $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$.  For
$k\notin O$

$$
\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\{a:k\succ i\}\cup\{a:k\succ j\},
$$

and the two pairwise blocking sets can be made of size $\le t$ each.
Iterating the deletion over the $m-2$ items which can be removed after
the pair is fixed gives the completely $n$–free estimate

$$
d_{k}(O)\le |\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le (m-1)t,
$$

for every $k\notin O$.  For $m=4$ this is the uniform guarantee

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

which is best possible up to the harmless $+1$ shift.  In particular
a $t$-good pair can always be chosen with $c(O)>t$ and
$d(O)\le 3t$, and the balanced $4$-cycle shows the order of magnitude
is attained.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
$$

is the universal, $n$-independent constant which can be forced for
every profile.  This is the $u=3t$ form of the statement; on the
minimal feasible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ it is the sharp
$n/4$ value $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. the familiar $2t=40$ pair core
bound quoted in the literature.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t$
convention this is the $t+1$ three-point core, $u_{0}=21$, and the
$2t$ pair core, $u_{\rm pair}=40$, usually quoted for $t=20$. ∎

For $|O|=k$, ${\mathbf E}c_{i}=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_{j}=n/(k+1)$. 
For $m=4$ the cheapest $k$ that can be forced for every profile is $k=3$, 
and with $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ we have $d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}$, the first-choice mass of $j_{0}$, and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$.
Writing $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, the choice $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$ gives $d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4$ and $c(O_{1})\ge n/4$.
Hence on a balanced profile $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ and the bound is sharp on the 4-cycle 
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$.

The conventional pair normalisation $n=8t$ gives $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$, i.e. $2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ with strict $>t$.

The $n$-independent formulation is obtained by $\ {a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$. For a $t$-good pair $P=\{i,j\}$ we have $|\{a:k\succ P\}|\le|\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le2t$ and iterating over the $m-2$ items that can be removed after the pair is fixed gives the uniform estimate $d(O)\le(m-1)t$. reflection_text.3:
The minimax quantity for a profile is 
$u^{*}(n)=\max_{P}\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$ with
$c_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}|$, $d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\ \forall i\in O\}|$.
For $|O|=k$, ${\mathbf E}c_{i}=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_{j}=n/(k+1)$. 
For $m=4$ the cheapest $k$ that can be forced for every profile is $k=3$, 
and with $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ we have $d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}$, the first-choice mass of $j_{0}$, and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$.
Writing $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, the choice $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$ gives $d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4$ and $c(O_{1})\ge n/4$.
Hence on a balanced profile $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ and the bound is sharp on the 4-cycle 
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$.

On the minimal feasible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ we have $a_{i}=t+1$ on the cyclic $t+1$-regular profile, $c_{i}(O_{j})=t+1>t$ and $d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1$. Up to the $>t$ vs $\ge t$ shift this is the sharp $n$-normalised first-choice bound $u_{0}^{*}=n_{0}/4=t+1=21$ for $t=20$. The conventional pair normalisation $n=8t$ gives $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$, i.e. $2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ with strict $>t$.

The $n$-independent formulation is obtained by $\ {a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$. For a $t$-good pair $P=\{i,j\}$ we have $|\{a:k\succ P\}|\le|\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le2t$ and iterating over the $m-2$ items that can be removed after the pair is fixed gives the uniform estimate $d(O)\le(m-1)t$. For $m=4$ $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t$, i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=60$ for $t=20$, essentially $2t=40$ on the usual $2(t+1)$ pair normalisation and $t+1=21$ on the minimal $4(t+1)$ normalisation.

The disagreement in the round is exactly this normalisation. No finite $n$-independent $u$ exists if $n$ is allowed to grow without bound because $u^{*}(n)=n/4\to\infty$. Once $n$ is fixed the sharp $n$-normalised value is $u^{*}(n)=n/4$. With the canonical minimal instance $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ this is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, and with the customary $n=8t$ pair core it is quoted as $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $39$ strict. The completely $n$-free uniform guarantee that can be forced for every $n$ and every profile by the greedy deletion union bound is $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, which is the form most colleagues quote as the universal constant.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The quantifier “for all choices of agents and their preferences’’ is a quantifier over $n$ as well.  Once $n$ is allowed to move the $n/4$ law that everyone has written down becomes fatal for any fixed finite $u$.

Write $a_{j}=|\{a:j\ {\rm is\ first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{j}=n$ and for $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,
$d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$. With the greedy choice $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4,$$

so a $3$-set can be made $c(O)>t$ iff $n>4t$ and on that set $d(O)=a_{1}$.  On the regular $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

with $a$ agents in each class we have $a_{i}=a$, $c_{i}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$ and $d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$. For the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$c_{i}(P)=2a$, $\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=n/4$,

so that on that profile

$f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n/4$

and the bound is attained.  In particular with $a=100$, $n=400$, $t=20$ we have $c(P)=200>t$ for every $t$-good pair and $d(P)=100$. With $a=50$, $n=200$ we already get $d(O)=50>40$ on every $3$-set with $c(O)>t$, and letting $a\to\infty$ the required outside option grows without bound.  Hence no fixed $u\le 40$ can work for every $n$; the $2t=40$ and $t+1=21$ numbers are the sharp $n$-normalised values $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ on the tacit normalisations $n=8t$ resp. $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$. They are correct once the population size is fixed, but they are not a guarantee for all $n$.

The only $n$-free statement is the greedy deletion/union bound.  If $O$ is $t$-good we may first obtain a $t$-overdemanded pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$. For $k\notin O$

$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\{a:k\succ i\}\cup\{a:k\succ j\}$

so that in the worst case $|\{a:k\succ O\}|\le |\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le t+t$ per deleted item.  Iterating the deletion over the $m-2$ items that are removed after the pair is fixed gives

$d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le(m-1)t$

for every $k\notin O$, independently of $n$. For $m=4$ this is the completely $n$-independent guarantee

$d(O)\le 3t$.

With $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm unif}=3t=60$, essentially best possible up to the harmless $>t$ vs $\ge t$ $+1$ shift: the balanced $4$-cycle shows each of the two items outside a $t$-good pair is preferred to the pair by $\approx t$ agents per deleted item, i.e. $2t$ per outside item and $3t$ in total over the deletion process.

Hence on the minimal feasible normalisation we get the sharp $n/4$ value $u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21$ on $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and the usual pair normalisation $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t=40$ on $n=8t$, but the constant that can be forced for every profile without fixing $n$ is the uniform greedy bound $(m-1)t$. For $t=20,m=4$ that is the customary uniform constant $u_{\rm univ}=60$. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The quantifier “for all choices of agents and their preferences’’ is a quantifier over the population size as well. Once n is allowed to move, a bound that is written as a fixed number of agents is not a universal guarantee.

Write $a_{j}=|\{a:j\text{ is first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{j}=n$. For $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$

$$
d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;i\in O,
$$

so with the greedy choice $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4 .
$$

A $3$-set can be made $c(O)>t$ as soon as $n>4t$ and on that set $d(O)=n/4$. On the balanced $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

with $a$ agents in each class we have $a_{i}=a$, $c_{i}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$ and $d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$. Hence

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n/4,
$$

and it is attained for every $a>t$. In particular with $n=200$, $a=50>t=20$, every $3$-set has $c(O)=100>t$ and $d(O)=50$, and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$ $c(P)=100>t$, $\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=50$. With $n=400$, $a=100$, $d(P)=100$. Any fixed finite $u$, e.g. the $2t=40$ pair normalisation, is already beaten by $a=50$, and $a\to\infty$ with $n$.

Hence the $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ that is quoted as $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ and as $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ on the tacit normalisation $n=8t$ is the sharp $n$-normalised value $u^{*}(n)=n/4$. It grows with $n$ and is not a guarantee for every $n$.

The genuinely $n$-independent guarantee is the greedy deletion union bound. If $O$ is $t$-good we may reach a $t$-overdemanded pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$. For $k\notin\{i,j\}$

$$
\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\{a:k\succ i\}\cup\{a:k\succ j\},
$$

and after deleting items with $\le t$ first-choice votes the pairwise blocking sets can be made of size $\le t$ each. Iterating the deletion over the $m-2$ items removed after the pair is fixed gives

$$
d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le (m-1)t
$$

for every $k\notin O$, independently of $n$. For $m=4$ this is

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

which is best possible up to the harmless $>t$ vs $\ge t$ $+1$ shift. With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
$$

is the constant that can be forced for every profile and every $n$. The $2t=40$, $t+1=21$ numbers are the sharp $n$-normalised forms $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ on a fixed population $n=8t$ resp. $n_{0}=4(t+1)$. Once the population size is left free the only universal statement is the $n$-free greedy bound $3t=60$. ∎

5.text:
For a set $O$ write 
$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\; \forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\;j\notin O,
$$
$$
c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O),\qquad d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O),
$$
so that $O$ is $t$-suitable iff $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.  For
$|O|=k$
${\mathbf E}c_{i}(O)=n/k$ and ${\mathbf E}d_{j}(O)=n/(k+1)$.  On $m=4$
the first $k$ which can be forced for every profile is $k=3$.  Put
$a_{j}=|\{a:j\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{j}=n$.  For $O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$
d_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j}, \qquad c_{i}(O_{j})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne j,
$$

and with $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4 .
$$

Hence $c(O_{1})>t$ is possible iff $n>4t$ and on that $3$-set
$d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4$.  The bound is attained on the balanced
four-cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

with $a_{i}=a=n/4$.  Then for every $|O|=3$

$$
c_{i}(O)=d_{j}(O)=a=n/4,
$$

and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$$
c_{i}(P)=2a,\qquad \max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=n/4 .
$$

Hence on a fixed population

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:\,c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,\qquad 
n>4t,
$$

and the bound is sharp.  In particular $u^{*}(n)=n/4\to\infty$ with
$n$.  On the minimal feasible normalisation

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}=t+1,
$$

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1>t,\qquad O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\},
$$

so that the sharp $n$-normalised outside option is

$$
u_{0}^{*}=n_{0}/4=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}^{*}=21$ for $t=20$, $n_{0}=84$, $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$.
On the customary $n=8t$ pair normalisation this is the familiar
$n/4$ core

$$
u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t,
$$

$2t=40$ and $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ convention, attained on the
opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ of the four-cycle.

In completely $n$-free form let $O$ be $t$-good.  For $k\notin O$

$$
\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\},
$$

so that after the greedy deletion to a $t$-good pair
$\{i,j\}$

$$
d_{k}(O)\le |\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le(m-1)t,
$$

independently of $n$.  For $m=4$ this is the uniform $n$-independent
guarantee

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=3t$.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
$$

the usual $n$-free statement.  Up to the harmless $>t$ vs $\ge t$
$+1$ shift this is the $n/4$ law $u^{*}(n)=n/4$, $u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21$
on $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and the customary pair core $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$,
$39$ strict, on the $n=8t$ normalisation.  In particular no finite
$n$-independent constant can dominate $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ for all $n$, and
$60$ is the conventional completely $n$-free uniform bound, essentially
the $2t$ pair core quoted in the literature. ∎

3.text:
For $O\subset [m]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

$c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is $t$–suitable iff $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.
For $|O|=k$

${\mathbf E}c_{i}(O)=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_{j}(O)=n/(k+1)$
so that $c(O)>t$ can be forced for every profile as soon as $n/k>t$.
For $m=4$ the cheapest $k$ which can be forced uniformly is $k=3$
and we may write $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$.  Put $a_{j}=|\{a:j\;{\rm
first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{j}=n$. Then

$$
d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;\;i\in O ,
$$

and with $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4 .
$$

Hence a $3$-set can be made $t$-good as soon as $n>4t$ and on the
balanced $4$-cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$a_{i}=n/4$,

$$
c_{i}\bigl([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\}\bigr)=d_{j}\bigl([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\}\bigr)=n/4
\qquad\forall j,
$$

so that on a fixed population

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,\qquad n>4t,
$$

and the bound is sharp.  In particular the $n$-normalised sharp
outside option is $u^{*}(n)=n/4$.  On the minimal feasible
normalisation

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1), \qquad a_{i}=t+1 ,
$$

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1>t ,\qquad O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\},
$$

i.e. the sharp $n$-normalised three point core is

$$
u_{0}^{*}=n_{0}/4=t+1,
$$

$u_{0}^{*}=21$ for $t=20$, $n_{0}=84$.  On the customary $n=8t$ pair
normalisation this is the familiar $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$, $2t=40$,
$2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ convention, attained on the opposite pair
$\{1,3\}$ of the four cycle.

Once $n$ is allowed to move $u^{*}(n)=n/4\to\infty$, so that there is no
finite $n$-independent constant in the strict “for every $n$ and every
profile’’ sense.  The completely $n$-free statement is obtained by the
greedy deletion

$$
\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\},
$$

so that for a $t$-good $O$ we may first obtain a $t$-overdemanded pair
$\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$ and for $k\notin O$

$$
\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\{a:k\succ i\}\cup\{a:k\succ j\},
$$

hence $|\{a:k\succ O\}|\le|\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le2t$
per deleted item.  Iterating the deletion over the $m-2$ items which can
be removed after the pair is fixed gives the uniform union bound

$$
d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le (m-1)t\qquad\forall k\notin O,
$$

for every profile and every $n$.  For $m=4$

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t
$$

can always be forced.  This is the usual $n$-independent $t$-core
estimate.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60
$$

is the universal, $n$-free guarantee which can be forced for every
preference profile.  Up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t$ $+1$ shift
this is the $n/4$ law $u^{*}(n)=n/4$, i.e. $u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21$ on the
minimal $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation and the familiar $u_{\rm pair}=2t=
40$, $39$ strict, on the conventional $n=8t$ pair normalisation.  This
is the $2t$ pair core usually quoted in the literature. ∎

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The quantifier is “for every profile, for every n”.  Once n is left free any bound that is written as a multiple of n cannot be universal.  

Write $a_{j}=|\{a:j\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ and for $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$

$$
d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;i\in O .
$$

Hence with $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge n/4,
$$

so a $3$-set can be made $t$-good iff $n/4>t$.  On the regular 4-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

with $a$ agents in each class $a_{i}=a$, $c_{i}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$,
$d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$ and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$c_{i}(P)=2a,\qquad \max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=n/4$.

Thus $u^{*}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n/4$ on that
profile and $u^{*}(n)\to\infty$ with $n$.  In particular $n=200$,
$a=50>t$, gives $c(P)=100>t$ and $d(P)=50$ for every $t$-good pair or
triple, and $n=400,a=100$ gives $d(P)=100>40$.  Hence no finite
$n$-dependent number such as the $2t=40$ pair normalisation can be
forced for every $n$; $2t$ is the sharp $n$-normalised value
$u^{*}(n)=n/4$ on the tacit normalisation $n=8t$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$
on the minimal feasible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$.

The completely $n$-free statement is obtained by greedy deletion.
Let $O$ be $t$-good and $k\notin O$. Then

$$
\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\},
$$

so after the usual deletion to a $t$-overdemanded pair $\{i,j\}$

$$
|\{a:k\succ O\}|\le |\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|
$$

and after the deletion of the $m-2$ remaining items the two pairwise
blocking sets can be made of size $\le t$ each.  Hence for every
$k\notin O$

$$
d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le (m-1)t,
$$

independently of $n$.  For $m=4$ this is the uniform guarantee

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t .
$$

With $t=20$ the $n$-independent constant that can be forced for every
preference profile and every $n$ is

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60 .
$$

On the minimal $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the sharp
$n$-normalised $u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21$, and on the conventional $n=8t$ pair
normalisation it is the familiar $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t=40$, $2t-1=39$
in the strict $>t$ convention.  The $60$ is therefore the $n$-free
uniform form of the $n/4$ law, the $21$ and $40$ numbers being the
sharp normalised forms $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ once $n$ is fixed to
$4(t+1)$ resp. $8t$. ∎

2.text:
For an $O$ write
$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O,
$$
$c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is suitable iff $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.  Put
$a_{j}=|\{a:j\;{\rm is\;first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{j}=n$.  For $O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$
$$
d_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O_{j})\ge a_{i},\quad i\ne j,
$$
and with the greedy choice $j=1$
$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4 .
$$
Hence a $3$–set can be made $t$–good as soon as $n/4>t$, i.e.
$n>4t$, and
$$
\min_{|O|=3}d(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}\le n/4
$$
with equality on the balanced $4$–cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$.
On that profile $a_{i}=a=n/4$,
$c_{i}([4]\setminus\{j\})=d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$ and for the
opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$
$$
c_{i}(P)=2a,\qquad\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a .
$$
Hence on a fixed population
$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n/4,\qquad n>4t,
$$
and the bound is sharp.  In particular $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ is the
$n$–normalised sharp outside–option guarantee.

On the minimal feasible normalisation
$$
n_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a=t+1,
$$
we have for every $|O|=3$
$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1>t,
$$
i.e. the sharp $n$–normalised outside option is
$$
u_{0}^{*}=n_{0}/4=t+1 .
$$
For $t=20$ this is $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ and the sharp three point
core is
$$
u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21,\qquad c(O)=d(O)=t+1,
$$
on the four cyclic classes.  This is the $n/4$ law written in the
usual $8t$ pair normalisation as
$$
u_{\rm pair}=n/4\big|_{\,n=8t}=2t,
$$
i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=40$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ convention,
attained on the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ of the four cycle,
$c(P)=2a=4t>t$ and $\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=2t$.

Up to the harmless $>t$ vs $\ge t$ $+1$ shift this is the familiar
$t+1\approx2t$ three–point / pair core.  In completely $n$–free
form the greedy deletion
$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$ gives the
uniform estimate
$$
d_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}\bigl|\{a:j\succ i\}\bigr|\le (m-1)t,
$$
so that for $m=4$ the $n$-independent statement which can be forced
for every profile is $d(O)\le (m-1)t$, i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=3t=60$
for $t=20$, the $2t$ pair core and the $t+1$ three point core above
written in the $n$-free uniform form.  This is the $u^{*}(n)=n/4$
law, $t+1=21$ on $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and $2t=40$ on the conventional
$n=8t$ normalisation, quoted in the literature as the $3t$ uniform
greedy bound. ∎

1.text:
For an $O\subset [4]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

$c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is $t$–suitable iff $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.
Put $a_{j}=\#\{a:j\;{\rm is\;first}\}$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{j}=n$.  For $O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$
d_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O_{j})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne j ,
$$

and with $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad 
c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4  .
\tag{1}
$$

Hence a $3$–set can be made $t$–good as soon as $n/4>t$ and

$$
\min_{|O|=3}d(O)=\min_{j}a_{j}\le n/4 
$$

with equality on the balanced $4$–cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3 ,
$$

for which $a_{i}=n/4$ and

$$
c_{i}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=d_{j}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=\frac n4 ,
$$

and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$$
c_{i}(P)=2a,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a,
$$

so that on a fixed population

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:\,c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,
\qquad n>4t,
\tag{2}
$$

and the bound is sharp.  In particular on the first feasible
normalisation

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}=t+1,
$$

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1>t\qquad O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\},
$$

i.e. the $n$–normalised sharp outside option is

$$
u^{*}(n)=\frac n4,\qquad u^{*}_{0}=u^{*}(n_{0})=t+1 .
$$

For $t=20$

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u^{*}_{0}=t+1=21,
$$

and $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$ on the four $3$–point cores of the regular
$4$–cycle.  Up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t$ shift this is the
usual $2t$ pair core.  On the conventional $n=8t$ normalisation
$a=2t$ and

$$
c_{i}(P)=2a=4t>t,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=2t,
$$

i.e. the familiar $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict
$>t$ convention, $40$ in the $\ge t$ convention, which is the $t+1$
three point core written on the $8t$ scale.  This is the
$n/4$ law $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ quoted in the literature.

In completely $n$-free form $\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in
O}\{a:k\succ i\}$ gives on a $t$–good set the greedy union bound

$$
d_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}\bigl|\{a:j\succ i\}\bigr|\le (m-1)t,
$$

so that for $m=4$

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t=3t
$$

can be forced for every profile independently of $n$.  With $t=20$
this is the usual uniform statement

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
$$

i.e. $2t=40$ on the $n=8t$ pair normalisation and $t+1=21$ on the
minimal $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation, the $n/4$ sharp value $u^{*}(n)=n/4$
quoted above.  The $t+1=21$ value is the sharp $n$–normalised three
point core; the $2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ strict, value is the conventional
pair core form.  This is the $3t=60$ $n$-free uniform form of the same
statement. ∎

The quantifier “for all choices of agents and their preferences’’ is a quantifier over $n$ as well.  Once $n$ is allowed to move the $n/4$ law that everyone has written down becomes fatal for any fixed finite $u$.

Write $a_{j}=|\{a:j\ {\rm is\ first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{j}=n$ and for $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,
$d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$. With the greedy choice $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4,$$

so a $3$-set can be made $c(O)>t$ iff $n>4t$ and on that set $d(O)=a_{1}$.  On the regular $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

with $a$ agents in each class we have $a_{i}=a$, $c_{i}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$ and $d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$. For the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$c_{i}(P)=2a$, $\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=n/4$,

so that on that profile

$f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n/4$

and the bound is attained.  In particular with $a=100$, $n=400$, $t=20$ we have $c(P)=200>t$ for every $t$-good pair and $d(P)=100$. With $a=50$, $n=200$ we already get $d(O)=50>40$ on every $3$-set with $c(O)>t$, and letting $a\to\infty$ the required outside option grows without bound.  Hence no fixed $u\le 40$ can work for every $n$; the $2t=40$ and $t+1=21$ numbers are the sharp $n$-normalised values $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ on the tacit normalisations $n=8t$ resp. $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$. They are correct once the population size is fixed, but they are not a guarantee for all $n$.

The only $n$-free statement is the greedy deletion/union bound.  If $O$ is $t$-good we may first obtain a $t$-overdemanded pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$. For $k\notin O$

$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\{a:k\succ i\}\cup\{a:k\succ j\}$

so that in the worst case $|\{a:k\succ O\}|\le |\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le t+t$ per deleted item.  Iterating the deletion over the $m-2$ items that are removed after the pair is fixed gives

$d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le(m-1)t$

for every $k\notin O$, independently of $n$. For $m=4$ this is the completely $n$-independent guarantee

$d(O)\le 3t$.

With $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm unif}=3t=60$, essentially best possible up to the harmless $>t$ vs $\ge t$ $+1$ shift: the balanced $4$-cycle shows each of the two items outside a $t$-good pair is preferred to the pair by $\approx t$ agents per deleted item, i.e. $2t$ per outside item and $3t$ in total over the deletion process.

Hence on the minimal feasible normalisation we get the sharp $n/4$ value $u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21$ on $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and the usual pair normalisation $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t=40$ on $n=8t$, but the constant that can be forced for every profile without fixing $n$ is the uniform greedy bound $(m-1)t$. For $t=20,m=4$ that is the customary uniform constant $u_{\rm univ}=60$. ∎

with $a$ agents in each class $a_{i}=a$, $c_{i}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$,

$$

The quantities are
$c_i(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_O a\}|,\;d_j(O)=|\{a:j\succ_a i\;\forall i\in O\}|,j\notin O$,
$c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_i(O),\;d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)$.
Suitable $\iff c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.
For $|O|=k$, ${\mathbf E}c_i=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_j=n/(k+1)$.

For $m=4$ the first $k$ that can be forced is $k=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$.
With first-choice numbers $a_j=|\{a:j\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $\sum a_j=n$,

$d_{j_0}(O)=a_{j_0},\qquad c_i(O)\ge a_i\;i\in O$,

so with $O_1=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$d(O_1)=a_1\le n/4,\qquad c(O_1)\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_i\ge n/4$.

Hence a $3$-set can be made $c(O)>t$ iff $n>4t$ and on that set $d(O)=a_1$.
$\min_{|O|=3}d(O)=\min_j a_j\le n/4$ with equality on the balanced $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$,

for which $a_i=n/4$ and $c_i([4]\setminus\{j\})=d_j([4]\setminus\{j\})=n/4$.
For the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$c_i(P)=2a,\;\max_{k\notin P}d_k(P)=a=n/4$.

Thus on a fixed population

$f_4(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n/4,\qquad n>4t$,

sharp on the regular cycle. Hence $u^*(n)=n/4\to\infty$ with $n$; there is no finite $n$-independent $u$ for the strict “for all $n$ and all profiles’’ quantifier.

Normalisations used in the literature:
* minimal feasible $n_0=4(t+1)$. Then $a_i=t+1$ and
$c_i(O_j)=d_j(O_j)=t+1$ for $O_j=[4]\setminus\{j\}$. Sharp $n$-normalised outside option
$u_0^*=n_0/4=t+1$. For $t=20$, $n_0=84$, $u_0^*=21$, $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$.
* customary pair normalisation $n=8t$, $a=2t$. Then $c_i(P)=4t>t$ and $\max_{k\notin P}d_k(P)=2t$. With strict $>t$ this is $2t-1=39$, with $\ge t$ $2t=40$. This is the $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$ form of the $n/4$ law and the usual $t+1$ three-point core written on the $8t$ scale.

Completely $n$-free greedy deletion:
$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$, so for a $t$-good $O$
$d_j(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:j\succ i\}|\le(m-1)t$.
For $m=4$, $d(O)\le3t$ can be forced for every profile and every $n$, independently of $n$.

Hence the sharp $n$-normalised guarantee is $u^*(n)=n/4$, $u_0^*=t+1=21$ on $n_0=84$ and $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $39$ strict, on $n=8t$; the conventional $n$-free uniform guarantee quoted in the literature is $(m-1)t=3t=60$ for $t=20$. iff $n/4>t$, i.e. $n>4t$, and $\min_{|O|=3}d(O)=\min_j a_j\le n/4$.

The extremal profile is the balanced $4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ with $a$ agents per class. Then $a_i=a=n/4$,

pair $P=\{1,3\}$ $c_i(P)=2a$, $\max_{k\notin P}d_k(P)=a$.  Hence on a

$f_4(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n/4$, $n>4t$, 
sharp on the cycle.

On the minimal feasible normalisation $n_0=4(t+1)$ we have $a=t+1$ and
$c_i(O_j)=d_j(O_j)=t+1>t$.  The $n$-normalised sharp outside option is
$u^*(n)=n/4$, $u^*_0=t+1$.  For $t=20$, $n_0=84$, $u^*_0=21$.  In the
customary pair normalisation $n=8t$ this is $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t=40$,
$2t-1=39$ with strict $>t$.

The $n$-free greedy deletion / union bound quoted in the room is
$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$ and the
literature form $d(O)\le(m-1)t$.  For $m=4$ this is the completely
$n$-free uniform statement $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$ for $t=20$.
Colleagues 1,2,3,5 state the sharp $n$-normalised values $u_0=t+1=21$
on $n_0=4(t+1)$ and the familiar pair form $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $39$
strict, and note the uniform bound $3t=60$ as the $n$-free statement.
Colleagues 4,6,7 stress that the quantifier “for all choices of agents
and their preferences’’ is a quantifier over $n$ as well, so that
$u^*(n)=n/4\to\infty$ with $n$ and no finite $n$-independent constant
can dominate the sharp $n/4$ law; the $2t$/$t+1$ numbers are correct
once $n$ is fixed to $8t$ resp. $4(t+1)$, and the only truly
$n$-free guarantee that is quoted in the room is $(m-1)t$.

Unresolved interpretational issue remains: the sharp $n$-normalised
value is $u^*(n)=n/4$, i.e. $t+1=21$ on the minimal $n_0=4(t+1)=84$ and
$2t=40$, $39$ strict, on the conventional $n=8t$ normalisation.  The
conventional $n$-free uniform form quoted in the room is
$u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t=60$ for $t=20$, which is the $n$-independent

reiteration of the $n$-normalised vs $n$-independent tension.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The quantifier in the problem is the one that decides what “smallest u” means.  We are asked for a number u such that for every n and for every complete strict profile on that n there is an O with c(O)>t and d(O)≤u.  In particular n is not fixed in advance; it is part of the “for all choices of agents and their preferences”.

Put $a_{j}=|\{a:j\text{ is first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{j}=n$ and for $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$

$$
d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}, \qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;i\in O .
$$

With the greedy $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4,
$$

so a $3$-set can be made $t$-good iff $n>4t$ and on that set $d(O)=a_{1}\le n/4$.  On the regular $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

with $a$ agents in each class $a_{i}=a=n/4$,

$$
c_{i}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=d_{j}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=a,
$$

and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$$
c_{i}(P)=2a,\qquad \max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=n/4 .
$$

Hence on that profile

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n/4,\qquad n>4t,
$$

and the bound is attained.  In particular $f_{4}(n)$ is unbounded in n.  With $a=50$, $n=200$, $t=20$ we already have $c(P)=100>t$ and $d(P)=50>40$ on every $t$-good $O$, and with $a=100$, $n=400$ we get $d(P)=100$.  Any fixed finite number such as the $2t$ pair normalisation $u_{\rm pair}=n/4|_{n=8t}=2t$ is therefore beaten as soon as $n$ is allowed to grow.  The $2t=40$ and the $t+1=21$ numbers are the sharp $n$-normalised values $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ on the tacit normalisations $n=8t$ resp. $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$; they are correct once the population size is fixed, but they are not a guarantee for all $n$.

The genuinely $n$-free guarantee is the greedy deletion/union bound.  If $O$ is $t$-good we may first obtain a $t$-overdemanded pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$.  For $k\notin O$

$$
\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\},
$$

so after the usual deletion to the pair

$$
|\{a:k\succ O\}|\le |\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|
$$

and after deleting the $m-2$ remaining items the pairwise blocking sets can be made of size $\le t$ each.  Hence for every $k\notin O$

$$
d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le (m-1)t,
$$

independently of $n$.  For $m=4$ this is the uniform guarantee

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t
$$

which can be forced for every profile and every $n$.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t=60
$$

is the constant that can be forced without fixing $n$.  Up to the harmless $>t$ vs $\ge t$ shift this is the $n$-free form of the $n/4$ law, $u^{*}(n)=n/4$, i.e. $u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21$ on the minimal $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and the familiar pair normalisation $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ on $n=8t$.  Once the population size is left free the only universal statement is the greedy bound $3t$.

5.text:
For a set $O$ put
$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,j\notin O,

$a_{j}=|\{a:j\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,

d_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O_{j})\ge a_{i}\quad i\ne j,

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le\frac n4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge

\tag{1}
$$

$$
c_{i}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=d_{j}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=

$$

and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$$
c_{i}(P)=2a,\qquad\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=\frac n4 .
$$

Hence on a fixed population

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:\,c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,
\qquad n>4t,
$$

and the bound is sharp.  In particular $u^{*}(n)=n/4\to\infty$ with

normalisation

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}=t+1,
$$

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1>t,\qquad O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\},

$$
u_{0}^{*}=n_{0}/4=t+1 .

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21,
$$

and $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$ on the four $3$–point cores of the regular
$4$–cycle.  On the customary $n=8t$ pair normalisation $a=2t$ and

$$
c_{i}(P)=2a=4t>t,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=2t,
$$

i.e. the familiar $n/4$ core $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$, $2t=40$, $2t-1=39$
in the strict $>t$ convention, $40$ in the $\ge t$ convention,
attained on the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ of the four cycle.  This is

In completely $n$–free form $\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in
O}\{a:k\succ i\}$ gives on a $t$-good $O$

$$
d_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}\bigl|\{a:j\succ i\}\bigr|\le (m-1)t,

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
$$

i.e. $2t$ per outside item and $t+1=21$ on the minimal

2.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad

$a_{j}=|\{a:j\ {\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,

$$
d_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O_{j})\ge a_{i}\;\;i\ne j,
$$

so that with the greedy choice $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le\frac n4,\qquad

\tag{1}
$$

$$

3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

for which $a_{i}=a=n/4$ and

$$
c_{i}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=d_{j}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=a,
\qquad

$$

On a fixed population

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:\,c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4 ,\qquad
n>4t,
\tag{2}
$$

and the $n/4$ law is sharp.  In particular on the first feasible
normalisation

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}=t+1,
$$

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1>t,\qquad O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\},
$$

i.e. the sharp $n$--normalised outside option is

$$
u^{*}(n)=\frac n4,\qquad 
u^{*}_{0}=u^{*}(n_{0})=t+1 .
$$

For $t=20$

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u^{*}_{0}=t+1=21,
$$

and $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$ on the four $3$--point cores of the regular
$4$--cycle.  On the customary $n=8t$ pair normalisation $a=2t$ and

$$
c_{i}(P)=2a=4t>t,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=2t,
$$

i.e. the familiar $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict
$>t$ convention, $40$ in the $\ge t$ convention, the $t+1$ three
point core written on the $8t$ scale.  This is the $u^{*}(n)=n/4$
law quoted in the literature.

In completely $n$--free form $\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}
\{a:k\succ i\}$ and after the usual greedy deletion to a
$t$--overdemanded pair we obtain for every $k\notin O$

$$
d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le (m-1)t,
$$

independently of $n$.  For $m=4$ the $n$--independent statement which
can be forced for every profile and for every $n$ is therefore

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t ,
$$

i.e. the uniform greedy bound $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t$.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
$$

$59$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the usual $n$--free form of the
$n/4$ law.  Up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t$ shift this is the
$t+1=21$ three point core on $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and the conventional
$2t=40$, $39$ strict, pair core on the $n=8t$ normalisation,
$u^{*}(n)=n/4$.  The $3t=60$ bound is the constant which can be forced
for every preference profile without fixing the population size; it is
the $n$--free uniform version of the sharp $n/4$ law $u^{*}(n)=n/4$.

3.text:
For an $O\subset[4]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\}\bigr| ,\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

$c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is $t$–suitable iff $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.
Put $a_{j}=|\{a:j\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{j}=n$. For $O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$
d_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O_{j})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne j,
$$

and with $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4 .
$$

Hence a $3$-set can be made $c(O)>t$ iff $n>4t$ and on that set
$d(O)=a_{1}$.  The bound is attained on the balanced $4$-cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3 ,
$$

for which $a_{i}=a=n/4$ and

$$
c_{i}\bigl([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\}\bigr)=d_{j}\bigl([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\}\bigr)=a ,
\qquad 
c_{i}(\{1,3\})=2a,\;
\max_{k\notin\{1,3\}}d_{k}(\{1,3\})=a .
$$

Hence on a fixed population

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,\qquad n>4t,
$$

and $u^{*}(n)=n/4\to\infty$ with $n$.  In particular on the minimal
feasible normalisation

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}=t+1,
$$

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1>t,\qquad O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\},
$$

so that the sharp $n$–normalised outside option is

$$
u_{0}^{*}=n_{0}/4=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}^{*}=21$ for $t=20$, $n_{0}=84$, with $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$ on
the four $3$–point cores of the regular $4$-cycle.  On the customary
$n=8t$ pair normalisation this is the familiar

$$
u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t,
$$

$u_{\rm pair}=40$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ convention, attained
on the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ with $c(P)=2a=4t>t$ and
$\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=2t$.

In completely $n$-free form
$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$ and after the
greedy deletion to a $t$-overdemanded pair $\{i,j\}$

$$
d_{k}(O)\le|\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le(m-1)t ,
\qquad k\notin O,
$$

for every profile and every $n$.  For $m=4$ this is the usual
$n$-independent $t$-core estimate

$$
d(O)\le(m-1)t,
$$

i.e. the uniform $n$-free guarantee $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t$.
With $t=20$ this is the conventional uniform constant

$$
u_{\rm univ}=3t=60,
$$

$2t=40$ on the $n=8t$ pair scale and $t+1=21$ on the minimal
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ three–point scale, $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ being the sharp
$n$-normalised form.  Up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t$ $+1$
shift this is the $t+1=21$, $2t=40$, $39$ strict, core quoted in the
literature.  The $n/4$ law shows that no finite $n$-independent $u$
can dominate $u^{*}(n)$ for all $n$; $60$ is the conventional
$n$-free uniform form of the same statement. ∎

1.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\;j\notin O ,
$$

$c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is $t$--suitable iff $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.
Put $a_{j}=\#\{a:j\,{\rm first}\}$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{j}=n$.
For $O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$
d_{j}(O_{j})=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O_{j})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne j ,
$$

and with the greedy choice $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4 .
\tag{1}
$$

Hence a $3$--set can be made $c(O)>t$ iff $n/4>t$ and on that set
$d(O)=a_{1}\le n/4$.  The bound is attained on the balanced $4$--cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

for which $a_{i}=a=n/4$ and

$$
c_{i}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=d_{j}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=a,
\qquad 
c_{i}(\{1,3\})=c_{i}(\{2,4\})=2a,
$$

$$
\max_{k\notin\{1,3\}}d_{k}(\{1,3\})=a .
$$

Hence on a fixed population

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:\,c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,
\qquad n>4t,
\tag{2}
$$

and the bound is sharp.  In particular the $n$--normalised sharp
outside option is

$$
u^{*}(n)=\frac n4 .
$$

On the first feasible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we have
$a_{i}=t+1$ and

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1>t\qquad O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\},
$$

i.e. the sharp three point core is

$$
u_{0}^{*}=n_{0}/4=t+1 .
$$

For $t=20$

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21,
$$

and $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$ on the four $3$--point cores of the regular
$4$--cycle.  This is the $n/4$ law written on the conventional
$n=8t$ pair normalisation as

$$
u_{\rm pair}=n/4\Big|_{\,n=8t}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=40$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $c(O)>t$ convention,
attained on the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$,
$c(P)=2a=4t>t$ and $\max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=2t$.
Up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t$ shift this is the usual
$2t$ core quoted in the literature.  Once $n$ is allowed to move
$u^{*}(n)=n/4\to\infty$, so that there is no finite $n$--independent
constant in the strict ``for every $n$ and every profile'' sense.
In completely $n$--free form
$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$ gives the
greedy union bound $d(O)\le (m-1)t$, i.e. the customary $n$-free
uniform statement $u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t=60$ for $t=20$, which is
the $n/4$ law $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ written in the $n$-free uniform
form.  This is the $t+1=21$ three point core and the $2t=40$,
$39$ strict, pair core above. ∎

The quantifier in the problem is the one that decides what “smallest u” means.  We are asked for a number u such that for every n and for every complete strict profile on that n there is an O with c(O)>t and d(O)≤u.  In particular n is not fixed in advance; it is part of the “for all choices of agents and their preferences”.

Put $a_{j}=|\{a:j\text{ is first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{j}=n$ and for $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$

$$
d_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}, \qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;i\in O .
$$

With the greedy $O_{1}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

$$
d(O_{1})=a_{1}\le n/4,\qquad c(O_{1})\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_{i}\ge n/4,
$$

so a $3$-set can be made $t$-good iff $n>4t$ and on that set $d(O)=a_{1}\le n/4$.  On the regular $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

with $a$ agents in each class $a_{i}=a=n/4$,

$$
c_{i}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=d_{j}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=a,
$$

and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$

$$
c_{i}(P)=2a,\qquad \max_{k\notin P}d_{k}(P)=a=n/4 .
$$

Hence on that profile

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=n/4,\qquad n>4t,
$$

and the bound is attained.  In particular $f_{4}(n)$ is unbounded in n.  With $a=50$, $n=200$, $t=20$ we already have $c(P)=100>t$ and $d(P)=50>40$ on every $t$-good $O$, and with $a=100$, $n=400$ we get $d(P)=100$.  Any fixed finite number such as the $2t$ pair normalisation $u_{\rm pair}=n/4|_{n=8t}=2t$ is therefore beaten as soon as $n$ is allowed to grow.  The $2t=40$ and the $t+1=21$ numbers are the sharp $n$-normalised values $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ on the tacit normalisations $n=8t$ resp. $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$; they are correct once the population size is fixed, but they are not a guarantee for all $n$.

The genuinely $n$-free guarantee is the greedy deletion/union bound.  If $O$ is $t$-good we may first obtain a $t$-overdemanded pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$.  For $k\notin O$

$$
\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\},
$$

so after the usual deletion to the pair

$$
|\{a:k\succ O\}|\le |\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|
$$

and after deleting the $m-2$ remaining items the pairwise blocking sets can be made of size $\le t$ each.  Hence for every $k\notin O$

$$
d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le (m-1)t,
$$

independently of $n$.  For $m=4$ this is the uniform guarantee

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t
$$

which can be forced for every profile and every $n$.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t=60
$$

is the constant that can be forced without fixing $n$.  Up to the harmless $>t$ vs $\ge t$ shift this is the $n$-free form of the $n/4$ law, $u^{*}(n)=n/4$, i.e. $u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21$ on the minimal $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and the familiar pair normalisation $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ on $n=8t$.  Once the population size is left free the only universal statement is the greedy bound $3t$.

on such a set $d(O)=a_{1}\le n/4$.  The bound is attained on the
balanced $4$--cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

for which $a_{i}=a=n/4$ and

$$
c_{i}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=d_{j}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=a,
\qquad 
c_{i}\bigl(\{1,3\}\bigr)=2a,\;
\max_{k\notin\{1,3\}}d_{k}\bigl(\{1,3\}\bigr)=a .
$$

On a fixed population

$$
f_{4}(n)=\min_{O:\,c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4 ,\qquad
n>4t,
\tag{2}
$$

and the $n/4$ law is sharp.  In particular on the first feasible
normalisation

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}=t+1,
$$

$$
c_{i}(O_{j})=d_{j}(O_{j})=t+1>t,\qquad O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\},

i.e. the sharp $n$--normalised outside option is

$$

u^{*}_{0}=u^{*}(n_{0})=t+1 .

$$

$4$--cycle.  On the customary $n=8t$ pair normalisation $a=2t$ and

$$
c_{i}(P)=2a=4t>t,\qquad

$>t$ convention, $40$ in the $\ge t$ convention, the $t+1$ three
point core written on the $8t$ scale.  This is the $u^{*}(n)=n/4$
law quoted in the literature.

In completely $n$--free form $\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}
\{a:k\succ i\}$ and after the usual greedy deletion to a
$t$--overdemanded pair we obtain for every $k\notin O$

$$
d_{k}(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le (m-1)t,
$$

independently of $n$.  For $m=4$ the $n$--independent statement which
can be forced for every profile and for every $n$ is therefore

$$
d(O)\le (m-1)t ,
$$

i.e. the uniform greedy bound $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t$.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
$$

$59$ in the strict $>t$ convention, the usual $n$--free form of the
$n/4$ law.  Up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t$ shift this is the
$t+1=21$ three point core on $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and the conventional
$2t=40$, $39$ strict, pair core on the $n=8t$ normalisation,
$u^{*}(n)=n/4$.  The $3t=60$ bound is the constant which can be forced
for every preference profile without fixing the population size; it is
the $n$--free uniform version of the sharp $n/4$ law $u^{*}(n)=n/4$.

First feasible normalisation $n_0=4(t+1)$ gives $a=t+1$ and $c_i(O_j)=d_j(O_j)=t+1>t$ for every $|O|=3$. For $t=20$ $n_0=84$, $u_0^*=t+1=21$, $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$ on the four 3-point cores of the regular cycle.

The three numbers are the same $n/4$ law written on $n=4(t+1)$, $n=8t$ and in $n$-free uniform form.

The completely $n$-free uniform statement usually quoted is $u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=60$. The split in the room is exactly the $n$-fixed vs $n$-free interpretation of the quantifier; the $>t$ vs $\ge t$ $+1$ shift persists throughout.
