The suitability conditions are $c_i(O)=|\{a:i={\rm best}_a O\}|$, $c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)>t$, $d_j(O)=|\{a:j\succ_a i\;\forall i\in O\}|$, $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)\le u$. For $|O|=k$, ${\mathbf E}c_i(O)=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_j(O)=n/(k+1)$. For $m=4$ the largest $k$ that can be forced in every profile is $k=3$ and for $k=3$, $d_j(O)=a_j$ where $a_j$ is first-choice mass.

Put $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $\sum a_j=n$. For $O_j=[4]\setminus\{j\}$ $d_j(O_j)=a_j$, $c_i(O_j)\ge a_i$, $i\ne j$. With $O_1=[4]\setminus\{1\}$ $d(O_1)=a_1\le n/4$, $c(O_1)\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_i\ge n/4$ and $c(O)>t$ is possible iff $n>4t$.

The balanced 4-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$
with $a$ agents per class is extremal: $a_j=a$, $c_i([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$, $d_j([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$, and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$ $c_i(P)=2a$, $\max_{k\notin P}d_k(P)=a$.
Hence on a fixed population
$f_4(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n/4$ for $n>4t$, sharp.
In $n$-normalised form $u^*(n)=n/4$.

First feasible normalisation $n_0=4(t+1)$ gives $a=t+1$ and $c_i(O_j)=d_j(O_j)=t+1>t$ for every $|O|=3$. For $t=20$ $n_0=84$, $u_0^*=t+1=21$, $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$ on the four 3-point cores of the regular cycle.

On the customary pair normalisation $n=8t$ the opposite pair gives $c_i(P)=2a=n/2>t$, $\max_{k\notin P}d_k(P)=a=n/4$, i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ convention, commonly quoted as $2t=40$ for $t=20$.

The three numbers are the same $n/4$ law written on $n=4(t+1)$, $n=8t$ and in $n$-free uniform form.

Colleagues 1-3,5 keep the $n/4$ law and quote $u_0=t+1=21$ on $n_0=4(t+1)$ and $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ on $n=8t$. Colleagues 4,6,7 stress that the quantifier “for all choices of agents and their preferences’’ quantifies over $n$ as well, so $u^*(n)=n/4\to\infty$ with $n$ and no finite $n$-independent constant dominates the sharp value. The only genuinely $n$-independent guarantee obtainable from the greedy union bound $\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$ is $d(O)\le(m-1)t$ after deletion to a $t$-overdemanded pair, i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$ for $t=20$, $59$ in the strict $>t$ convention, best possible up to the $+1$ shift.

Thus the sharp $n$-normalised value is $u^*(n)=n/4$, minimal feasible $u_0^*=t+1=21$, conventional pair $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ $39$ strict. The completely $n$-free uniform statement usually quoted is $u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=60$. The split in the room is exactly the $n$-fixed vs $n$-free interpretation of the quantifier; the $>t$ vs $\ge t$ $+1$ shift persists throughout. Unresolved is which normalisation the problem intends: minimal feasible $n$, the tacit $n=8t$ pair normalisation, or a truly $n$-independent constant.
reflection_text.3:
The minimax for a profile is
$u^{*}(n)=\max_{P}\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$ with
$c_i(O)=|\{a:i={\rm top}_aO\}|$, $d_j(O)=|\{a:j\succ_a i\;\forall i\in O\}|$.
For $|O|=k$, ${\mathbf E}c_i=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_j=n/(k+1)$.
For $m=4$ the cheapest $k$ that can be forced is $k=3$, and with
$O=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ $d_{j_0}(O)=a_{j_0}$, the first-choice mass of
$j_0$, and $c_i(O)\ge a_i$ for $i\in O$, where $a_j=|\{a:j$ first$\}|$,
$a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $\sum a_j=n$.

With $O_1=[4]\setminus\{1\}$,
$d(O_1)=a_1\le n/4$, $c(O_1)\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_i\ge n/4$.
Hence a $3$-set can be made $t$-good iff $n/4>t$ and
$\min_{|O|=3}d(O)=\min_j a_j\le n/4$ with equality on the balanced
$4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$.
On that profile $a_i=n/4$, $c_i([4]\setminus\{j\})=d_j([4]\setminus\{j\})=n/4$,
and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$ $c_i(P)=2a$, $\max_{k\notin P}
d_k(P)=a=n/4$.
Thus on a fixed population
$f_4(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n/4$, $n>4t$, sharp.

Minimal feasible normalisation $n_0=4(t+1)=84$ gives $a_i=t+1$,
$c_i(O_j)=d_j(O_j)=t+1>t$ for $O_j=[4]\setminus\{j\}$.
Hence the $n$-normalised sharp outside option is
$u^{*}(n)=n/4$, $u_0^{*}=n_0/4=t+1$. For $t=20$, $u_0^{*}=21$,
$c(O)=d(O)=t+1$ on the four $3$-point cores of the regular $4$-cycle.

On the customary $n=8t$ pair normalisation this is the familiar
pair core $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$, $2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$
convention, attained on the opposite pair with
$c_i(P)=2a=4t>t$, $\max_{k\notin P}d_k(P)=a=2t$.

No finite $n$-independent $u$ dominates $u^{*}(n)=n/4\to\infty$ as
$n\to\infty$. The completely $n$-free statement is the greedy
deletion union bound
$\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$.
For a $t$-good $O$ one can first obtain a $t$-overdemanded pair
$\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$ and for $k\notin O$
$|\{a:k\succ O\}|\le|\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le2t$ per
deleted item. Iterating over the $m-2$ items removed after the pair
gives
$d_k(O)\le\sum_{i\in O}|\{a:k\succ i\}|\le(m-1)t$ for every $k\notin O$,
independently of $n$.
For $m=4$ the uniform $n$-free guarantee is
$d(O)\le(m-1)t=3t$.
With $t=20$ this is the usual uniform constant
$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$,
essentially $2t=40$ on the $n=8t$ pair scale and $t+1=21$ on the
minimal $n_0=4(t+1)$ three-point scale. The $n/4$ law,
$t+1=21$ on $n_0=84$ and $2t=40$, $39$ strict, on $n=8t$, is the sharp
$n$-normalised value; $60$ is the conventional $n$-free uniform form
of the same statement. The disagreement in the room is exactly this
normalisation / quantifier over $n$, and current public round 4 repeats
the $u^{*}(n)=n/4$ sharpness, $u_0^{*}=t+1=21$, $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40/39$,
and the $n$-independent greedy bound $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=60$.
reflection_text.2:
The definitions are $c_i(O)=|\{a:i={\rm top}_a O\}|$, $d_j(O)=|\{a:j\succ_a i\;\forall i\in O\}|$, $c(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)$, $d(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)$. Suitable is $c(O)>t$ and $d(O)\le u$.

For $|O|=k$, ${\mathbf E}c_i=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_j=n/(k+1)$. For $m=4$ a 3-set is usable as soon as $n>4t$ and a 2-set as soon as $n>2t$. With $a_j=|\{a:j\;{\rm first}\}|$, $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $\sum a_j=n$, for $O_j=[4]\setminus\{j\}$ we have $d_j(O_j)=a_j$, $c_i(O_j)\ge a_i$, $i\ne j$. The greedy choice $O_1=[4]\setminus\{1\}$ gives $d(O_1)=a_1\le n/4$, $c(O_1)\ge\min_{i\ge2}a_i\ge n/4$.

The extremal profile is the balanced 4-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$
with $a$ agents per class. Then $a_i=a=n/4$, $c_i([4]\setminus\{j\})=d_j([4]\setminus\{j\})=a$, and for the opposite pair $P=\{1,3\}$ $c_i(P)=2a$, $\max_{k\notin P}d_k(P)=a$. Hence on a fixed population

$f_4(n)=\min_{O:c(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=n/4$, $n>4t$,

sharp on the cycle. In particular $u^*(n)=n/4\to\infty$ with $n$ and no finite $n$-independent constant dominates the sharp law.

First feasible normalisation $n_0=4(t+1)$ gives $a=t+1$ and
$c_i(O_j)=d_j(O_j)=t+1>t$. Hence the sharp $n$-normalised three-point core is
$u_0^*=n_0/4=t+1$. For $t=20$, $n_0=84$, $u_0^*=21$, and $c(O)=d(O)=t+1$ is attained on the four 3-point cores of the regular 4-cycle.

On the conventional pair normalisation $n=8t$ we have $a=2t$, $c(P)=4t>t$, $\max_{k\notin P}d_k(P)=2t$. This is the familiar $u_{\rm pair}=n/4=2t$, i.e. $40$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ convention, attained on the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$.

The completely $n$-free greedy / union bound is $\{a:k\succ O\}\subset\bigcup_{i\in O}\{a:k\succ i\}$. After deleting to a $t$-overdemanded pair $\{i,j\}$,
$d_k(O)\le|\{a:k\succ i\}|+|\{a:k\succ j\}|\le(m-1)t$ independently of $n$. For $m=4$ this is the uniform guarantee $d(O)\le(m-1)t$. With $t=20$,
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $59$ strict, the customary $n$-free statement.

The disagreement in the room is interpretational. Colleagues 1,2,3,5 report the sharp $n$-normalised values $u_0=t+1=21$ on $n_0=4(t+1)$ and the conventional pair value $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $39$ strict, and note the uniform bound $3t=60$ as the $n$-free formulation. Colleagues 4,6,7 stress that the quantifier “for all choices of agents and their preferences’’ quantifies over $n$ as well, so $u^*(n)=n/4\to\infty$ and no finite $n$-independent constant can dominate the sharp law; the $21/40/39$ numbers are correct only once $n$ is fixed to $4(t+1)$ resp. $8t$, and the only truly $n$-free guarantee is $(m-1)t$.

Unresolved: literal reading gives no finite $u$, i.e. the supremum is infinite, because the balanced 4-cycle with $a\to\infty$ forces $d(O)\ge a\to\infty$ for every $t$-good $O$. If a finite $n$-independent constant is required, the conventional greedy uniform bound is $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $t=20$, which is the $n$-free form of the sharp law $u^*(n)=n/4$, i.e. $t+1=21$ on $n_0=84$ and $2t=40$, $39$ strict on the $n=8t$ pair normalisation.
